analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the ban on exporting U.S.-produced crude oil and natural gas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee until the 118th Congress ended, with 1 sponsor and 7 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Until 2015, federal law banned exporting most American crude oil. This bill would reinstate that ban, requiring the President to write a rule prohibiting exports of U.S.-produced crude oil and natural gas, with exemptions only where the President finds them consistent with the national interest. It also gives the President discretionary authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks. The stated idea is to keep America's energy supply at home instead of selling it abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: American households and businesses that buy energy, since keeping crude oil and natural gas in the domestic market would put more supply where American buyers are bidding, and U.S. allies of the climate cause who want fossil fuels left unburned. Gas-dependent manufacturers and utilities would also benefit from a larger domestic gas supply.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to issue a rule prohibiting exports of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, reversing the 2015 repeal of the export ban.
Exemptions from the ban are allowed only if the President finds the specific exports consistent with the national interest, and any exemption must be written into the rule or an amendment to it.
The bill preserves cross-border energy trade with Canada and Mexico, so historical trading relationships are not interrupted.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would lose access to foreign markets that pay world prices, and any refiners, shippers, and terminal operators built around the export trade. If the President uses the discretionary authority, coal exporters and petrochemical feedstock exporters could also lose markets.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers all U.S.-produced crude oil and natural gas, so producers would lose export revenue, which could reduce drilling and production over time and slightly shrink total supply.

The bill gives the President sweeping authority to restrict not just oil and gas but coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks, with only loose guardrails, an unusually broad delegation of trade power to the executive.
The President may waive the normal public notice-and-comment process if acting quickly is needed to impose the ban, limiting public input on a major economic rule.
Allies in Europe and Asia that came to rely on U.S. natural gas exports could lose supply, since exemptions are granted only at the President's discretion on a case-by-case basis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims a real benefit at energy consumers and leans against fossil fuel expansion, but it is a blunt tool. Cutting off export markets would squeeze domestic producers hard, and it is contested among economists how much export bans actually lower domestic prices; some of the lost export revenue would come back as lower domestic revenue to the same companies. The breadth of the President's new restriction authority is a legitimate structural concern. Reasonable people can weigh consumer and climate benefits against those costs; the bill never got that debate, because it never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Adriano Espaillat introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, joined by Reps. Clarke, Huffman, and Brownley as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which then sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security the next day.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the action history ends at the subcommittee referral.
Seven additional members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, and no version of it advanced in the House or the Senate before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas exporters, who kept full access to overseas markets that pay world prices, and the export terminals and shipping businesses built around that trade.

for.name: Rep. Adriano Espaillat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the ban on crude oil and natural gas exports.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke, Jared Huffman, and Julia Brownley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Four additional House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors after introduction, bringing the total to 8 including the sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill went no further than a subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no voting breakdown exists; its support was entirely Democratic — a Democratic sponsor and 7 Democratic cosponsors — with no Republican backing in the record.

industries.industry: Crude oil and natural gas producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill would cut them off from export markets that pay world prices, ending the trade that became a major profit channel after the export ban was lifted in 2015. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the bill's aim of keeping more energy supply in the domestic market for American buyers.
The bill does not ban their exports outright, but gives the President standing authority to restrict them. That threat hangs over their markets without imposing a definite rule.

industries.industry: Gas- and oil-dependent manufacturers and utilities
industries.note: Keeping more domestic oil and gas inside the U.S. market would increase the supply available to American factories, power plants, and utilities that buy it as an input or a fuel.
